subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Mental Accounting
description: A micro-lesson that makes Mental Accounting usable.

hook.text: You won't pay $20 for a new movie ticket after losing one. But you'll buy it if you lost a $20 bill. Same loss.

buildup.text: Thaler's mental accounting: we sort money into separate mental categories, treating each with different rules.

discovery.text: Money is fungible, but we treat the entertainment budget differently from the grocery budget. Each has its own pain.

twist.text: Tax refunds feel like bonus money and get spent freely. But it was your own money all along, just returned late.

climax.text: Mental accounts simplify life. But they also make us irrational: paying credit card interest while keeping savings.

punchline.text: A dollar is a dollar, but your brain disagrees.

quiz.question: What is mental accounting?
options: Using a professional accountant for taxes
Treating money differently depending on mental category
Keeping exact records of all expenses

details.summary: Mental accounting is the tendency to categorize money into separate mental accounts for different purposes, treating dollars differently based on their source or intended use rather than recognizing that all money is fungible.
details.whyItMatters: Mental accounting explains why people spend tax refunds frivolously while hoarding savings, or why they carry credit card debt while keeping low-interest savings. It reveals that humans do not treat money as the interchangeable resource it is.
takeaways: People assign money to mental categories like savings, fun, and bills
Money is treated differently based on its source or designated purpose
Mental accounting violates the economic principle of fungibility

faq.question: Why do people treat windfall money differently from earned money?
faq.answer: Windfall money goes into a mental 'bonus' account with looser spending rules. Earned income goes into a more carefully guarded account. The same $500 is spent casually as a gift but carefully as wages, despite being economically identical.

faq.question: Can mental accounting ever be helpful?
faq.answer: Yes. Budgeting is a form of mental accounting that helps control spending. Designating money for specific purposes like emergency funds or retirement creates psychological barriers against raiding those accounts for impulse purchases.
